Creating a Pixel Art Scene in Realtime 3D

For the past few weekends, I've been working on a game engine that runs custom shader code on the GPU to turn plain-looking 3D objects into a beautiful scenic pixel-art environment.

This is the result so far, and here's how I made it.

First some proof that the scene is indeed 3D, and looks consistent from different viewing angles.

The first step is to build the objects in the scene. I threw this together fairly quickly in Blender, which is a popular (free!) 3D modeling software. While modeling, I take care to keep things aligned to 45 degree angles whenever possible: this will pay off in the final image, because 45 degree angles look especially pleasing when viewed from the isometric pixel art perspective.

In the game engine (Unity3D), after loading the model from Blender, I add some hilly terrain, and a sun to provide some crisp directional lighting.

At this stage, I add some cartoon shading with a fairly standard toon shader: each material has an adjustable highlight, midtone, and shadow color, and some settings for how smoothly to blend between the different colors.

When I press play, the game engine will randomly add grass sprites all over the grassy parts of the terrain. Each grass sprite is shaded with the same toon coloring as the terrain it sits on, which results in this effect where the boundaries between colors get broken up by a grassy pattern.

To help add visual interest and to break up the colors a bit more, I drape some procedurally generated shadows over the scene, to simulate cloud coverage or a forest canopy. The extra shadows cause the effect of the grass sprites to really come alive.

To sell the isometric pixel art look, we need to highlight the outward-facing edges, and darken the outlines of objects a bit. To do this, we first tell the GPU to compute a depth pass and normal pass, which carry information about how far away neighboring pixels are, and what direction they are facing. Using this information, the shader code can determine whether each pixel lies on an edge or not. The main challenge at this stage is to get every edge pixel exactly perfect, or else the pixel art effect will be lost.

In general, the edge detection shader needs to produce clean single-pixel lines for objects of all shapes, sizes, and orientations.

To complete the scene, I added a water surface that moves up and down. The water effect is a pretty standard mix of refraction, reflection, and texture displacement to simulate ripples.

The most important detail for the pixel art aesthetic is to draw a single pixel highlight on the border between the water and air. This is done using the same pixel art edge detector as earlier.

For me, the most exciting part of this project is just how easy it is to iterate on the look of a scene. For example, this nighttime version was made just by swapping a few color palettes and adding a dynamic light.
